title: What the Energy Crunch Means for Winter Bills
standfirst: A plain guide to the price cap, and who is most exposed.
body: Every autumn the same question comes round: what will heating the house cost this winter? The answer depends on forces a long way from your front door, and on a regulated limit that is often misunderstood.
## What the price cap is, and is not

The price cap does not limit your bill. It limits the rate a supplier can charge for each unit of energy, and the daily standing charge, for customers on a standard tariff. Use more and you pay more. A cold winter can raise a household bill sharply even if the cap does not move at all.

The cap is reset every few months to follow wholesale prices, with a delay. When wholesale gas rises, the cap follows some months later. When it falls, bills take time to come down too. That lag is why bills can feel out of step with the headlines.

Britain heats most of its homes with gas, and it buys much of that gas on international markets. A cold snap in Asia, a supply problem in Norway or trouble on a shipping route can all push prices up. The market does not care that the buyer is a pensioner in Doncaster.

The households that suffer most are not always the poorest on paper. They are the ones with poorly insulated homes, people who are at home all day, and anyone using a prepayment meter, which can cost more per unit. Older people living alone in large, draughty houses are especially exposed.

Check that you are on the right tariff, and whether a fixed deal makes sense. Bleed the radiators, draught-proof the doors and turn the boiler flow temperature down a little. None of this solves the larger problem, but it can take a real amount off a winter bill.
